title: Breweries and wineries: what to expect

sections.h: A younger scene than the golf or the boardwalk
p: South Carolina loosened its brewery rules in the early 2010s, which made it much easier for small breweries to serve full pints and food. The Grand Strand's scene grew from there. New South Brewing in Myrtle Beach is one of the longest-running names, and Visit Myrtle Beach now publishes a Beer Trail that covers roughly ten breweries, many of which are on this page.

Wine here leans toward muscadine, the sweet native grape of the Southeast. Duplin Winery, La Belle Amie and Carolina Vineyards are the places to try it, and wine bars like Bin 2004 and The Tasting Room on 9th pour wines from farther afield.

sections.h: How to do a brewery day
p: Breweries are spread out. A few sit near Broadway at the Beach and the Myrtle Beach airport, others are in North Myrtle Beach, and Winyah Bay Brewing is in Georgetown. If you want to visit more than two in a day, group them by area instead of crossing the Strand twice.

Many tasting rooms are in industrial or commercial buildings rather than on the beach, so the scenery is not the draw. The beer, the patio and the crowd are. Check each brewery's own page before you go, since taproom hours and food trucks change.

list: Tasting rooms often have limited weekday hours, especially in winter. Call ahead.
Some breweries do not serve food and rely on food trucks or let you bring your own. Others have a full kitchen.
Take-home beer is limited by state rules, and the allowed amount has changed in recent years, so ask what you can buy to go.
Plan a ride or a designated driver. Alcohol is also not allowed on most area beaches, so save the tasting for after you leave the sand.
